Aadit Solar: The App Nobody Opens

Ahmedabad, October 2025. A rooftop-solar company must decide whether its customers are disengaged, or simply have nothing to do.

1. Seven days to the plan

On the evening of 30 September 2025, Sneha Deshmukh stayed back in Aadit Solar's office on Ashram Road in Ahmedabad after the Bengaluru engineers had signed off and before the Toronto data scientist came online. She had until 7 October — a fortnight before Diwali, when the whole company would effectively stop for ten days — to submit the FY27 product plan.

The founder, Vikram Sheth, had already told her what he wanted in it. Aadit's homeowner app, Aadit Home, had a DAU/MAU of 6 per cent. Vikram wanted ₹6 crore allocated to an engagement programme — a daily energy feed, a neighbourhood leaderboard, carbon-saving badges, a Diwali "clean energy" campaign — with a target of 20 per cent by the end of FY27. He had a Series C conversation beginning in January and a slide that currently read badly.

Sneha had a different set of numbers from Farah Qureshi in Toronto, and they suggested that Aadit's customers were not disengaged at all. They simply did not have twenty days' worth of business a month with a solar rooftop.

2. Company background

Aadit Solar was founded in 2019 in Ahmedabad to sell, install and maintain residential rooftop solar systems. By September 2025 it had installed 68,000 systems across Gujarat, Rajasthan, Maharashtra and Karnataka, averaging 4.2 kW per home, at an installed price of about ₹2.1 lakh before subsidy. Revenue for FY25 was ₹412 crore, of which installation was ₹388 crore and service contracts the remainder.

The business had been transformed by the PM Surya Ghar Muft Bijli Yojana, the central rooftop subsidy scheme launched in February 2024, which routed a direct benefit transfer to the homeowner and pushed state DISCOMs to clear net-metering applications faster. Aadit competed with Tata Power Solar's residential network, with local installers using panels from Waaree, Vikram Solar and Adani Solar, and increasingly with financing-led offers from banks and NBFCs. Its differentiator, from the beginning, had been software: every Aadit system shipped with a monitoring gateway, and every homeowner got Aadit Home, which showed generation, estimated savings, subsidy status and service history, and took payments over UPI.

The software had also become a small second business. Rajat Nair, based in Singapore, ran partnerships, and had licensed a white-labelled version of the monitoring platform to three engineering-procurement-construction firms, including Mirath Energy Services in Dubai, which used it across 900 commercial rooftops in the UAE. That line billed ₹9 crore a year and was growing.

3. The situation

The concern had started with a cohort chart. In the first month after commissioning, 94 per cent of homeowners opened the app and the average household opened it on nine days. By month four, monthly openers had fallen to 41 per cent and average days to 1.6. By month twelve, 29 per cent and 1.2. Blended across the installed base, that produced the 6 per cent that Vikram disliked.

Lukas Brenner, Aadit's designer in Berlin, had read the same chart as a product failure and produced, unprompted, a twelve-screen concept for a gamified feed with streaks, a society-level leaderboard and shareable badges. It was well made, and Vikram had shown it twice to the leadership team.

Farah, in Toronto, had approached it differently. Instead of asking why homeowners stopped opening the app, she asked what a homeowner actually needed from a rooftop system in a year, and then measured the gaps between consecutive sessions. The gap distribution had a hard spike at 28 to 34 days — the DISCOM billing cycle, when a homeowner receives the electricity bill and wants to check whether the solar savings match — a second cluster in the week following any generation anomaly, and almost nothing in between. Her note to Sneha, sent at 02:10 India time, said: "The app has a monthly heartbeat because the bill is monthly. There is no daily job here. The question is not how often they come; it is whether we are there on the days they need us."

There was one more finding, and it was the uncomfortable one. Of the 4,100 systems that had experienced a material generation shortfall in the June-to-September monsoon quarter — soiling, a shaded string, a failed optimiser, an inverter fault — only 38 per cent of the households had raised a service request within thirty days. The rest had lost generation silently, at an average of ₹640 a month. Anitha Balan, who ran field service from Bengaluru, had been saying for a year that she could not fill her technicians' schedules even as the installed base grew.

4. The people

Vikram Sheth, founder and chief executive, Ahmedabad. He wanted a defensible engagement story for the Series C and believed that a solar app could become a home-energy habit the way payments apps had become a daily habit. He had raised ₹210 crore across two rounds and had eleven months of runway at current burn.

Sneha Deshmukh, head of product, Ahmedabad. Four years at Aadit, previously at a consumer lending product in Mumbai. She had to sign the plan and would own the metric whichever way it went.

Farah Qureshi, data scientist, Toronto. Wanted the company to adopt an occasion-based measure and was, by her own admission, unbothered by how the slide looked to investors.

Anitha Balan, head of field service, Bengaluru. Wanted proactive fault detection and one-tap service booking, because her margin depended on route density and her technicians were at 54 per cent utilisation. She was sceptical of anything that added notifications without adding jobs.

Rajat Nair, partnerships and customer success, Singapore. Wanted engineering capacity for the EPC platform, where installers logged in every working day and where Mirath Energy Services in Dubai had asked for multi-site alarm routing as a condition of renewing a ₹4.2 crore contract in April 2026.

5. Exhibits

Exhibit 1. Aadit Home engagement by months since commissioning, September 2025 (n = 68,000 systems).

Source: Aadit product analytics. "Opened app in month" counts any session; DAU/MAU uses mean daily sessions over a 30-day calendar month. Installations before FY23 excluded from the 12–35 band where gateways were not fitted.

Exhibit 1 is the chart Vikram read as decay and Farah read as a product settling onto its natural rhythm. The first month is genuinely different: subsidy paperwork, net-metering approval and the novelty of watching a meter run backwards. After that, the mean settles at roughly one and a half days a month — which, read against a thirty-day month, is arithmetically about 5 per cent whatever the design team does.

Exhibit 2 is the heart of the case. A rooftop system generates a job for its owner about sixteen times a year. If Aadit captured every one of those occasions perfectly and the homeowner opened the app on exactly one day for each, the DAU/MAU would be about 4.5 per cent. The company was already at six. There was no twenty per cent available without inventing occasions that did not exist in the customer's life.

Exhibit 3 says that the engagement problem Aadit actually had was not on the sixteen days when customers wanted the app. It was on the roughly 2,500 households a quarter who had a fault and never learned about it. Raising AMC attach from 11 to 25 per cent on the installed base would be worth about ₹33 crore a year, and every point of attach also filled Anitha's technician routes.

6. The options

Option A — Build for engagement. Fund Lukas's concept at ₹6 crore: daily energy feed, society leaderboards, badges, a Diwali campaign, with push notifications to drive daily opens. The upside is a metric that will almost certainly move, an investor narrative about a home-energy habit, and a possible referral channel through leaderboard sharing. The cost is two quarters of the Bengaluru and Pune teams, a notification budget spent on messages of no economic value, and the risk that the engagement messages crowd out the fault alerts that matter.

Option B — Build for the occasions. Spend ₹3.5 crore rebuilding the app around the sixteen occasions: a monthly savings digest timed to each DISCOM's billing date, automatic shortfall detection with a one-tap service booking, a pre-monsoon and post-monsoon cleaning prompt, and a net-metering tracker. Report occasion capture rate and days-to-fix as the headline metrics; accept that DAU/MAU stays near 7 per cent. The upside is AMC attach, technician utilisation and customer savings. The cost is that Vikram has no engagement story in January, and that the work depends on field-operations execution outside Sneha's control.

Option C — Follow the frequency to the installers. Redirect the engineering capacity to the EPC platform Rajat sells, where installers and site managers genuinely work in the product every day, and where Mirath Energy Services in Dubai has asked for multi-site alarm routing. The upside is a daily-use product with honest stickiness, a ₹9 crore line that could plausibly triple, and enterprise contracts with visible renewal economics. The cost is that the consumer app is left as it is, the field-service opportunity goes unaddressed, and Aadit begins to split its identity between a consumer brand and a software vendor.

7. Questions for discussion

1. Using Exhibit 1 and Exhibit 2, what is the natural frequency of the job Aadit Home performs, and what DAU/MAU would a perfectly executed version of the app achieve?

2. Vikram's benchmark comes from consumer apps he uses daily. What would make a comparison set fair for Aadit, and what number should he take to the Series C instead?

3. Exhibit 3 describes a failure of engagement on days when customers genuinely needed the product. How would you measure that failure, and what target would you set for FY27?

4. Which option should Sneha put in the plan on 7 October, and what single metric should she ask to be held to?

8. A note for the learner

The lens for this case is the relationship between stickiness and natural frequency. DAU/MAU is a ratio with a simple arithmetic meaning — the average number of days a month a user is active, divided by the days in the month — and it is only interpretable against how often the underlying problem occurs. Aadit's 6 per cent is 1.8 days out of thirty. Exhibit 2 establishes that a rooftop system creates about sixteen occasions a year, or 1.3 a month. Read together, the two say that Aadit is capturing most of the occasions available to it. The product is not failing to engage; it is being measured on a scale built for a different kind of problem.

A well-reasoned answer will do three things. It will compute the ceiling explicitly rather than asserting that the target is unrealistic. It will distinguish clearly between raising frequency by adding genuine jobs to a customer's life — which Option B does modestly, by making cleaning and fault resolution into real occasions — and manufacturing frequency through mechanics unconnected to value, which is what Option A does. And it will replace the metric rather than merely rejecting the target, because a product leader who takes a number away from a chief executive without offering a better one will lose the argument.

One defensible path is Option B, with two modifications. First, Sneha should propose occasion capture rate as the headline engagement metric — the share of a household's identified occasions in which the household completed the relevant action in the app — with a baseline of 38 per cent on fault events and a target of 70 per cent for FY27, alongside AMC attach rising from 11 to 20 per cent. Second, she should keep DAU/MAU on the dashboard, demoted to a diagnostic, and replace it in the investor deck with a monthly figure: MAU as a share of the installed base, currently 39 per cent, which is a genuinely strong number for a product with a monthly job. That reframing gives Vikram a better slide than the one he has, because it is defensible under questioning.

Option C is not wrong, and a class that argues for it is arguing something serious: if Aadit wants a daily-use product, it should build for users whose work is daily. The strongest version of that argument treats Option C as a parallel bet funded from the ₹6 crore rather than a replacement for serving homeowners. Option A is the option that should be hardest to defend, not because gamification never works, but because in this case it would spend two quarters and a scarce notification budget to move a number that, by Exhibit 2, cannot rise to the target without the customer's life changing first.

Pahiya: The Frequency Ladder

Gurugram, the night of Sunday 16 November 2025. A used-car company must tell its board on Monday what business it is in.

1. Sunday night

Aditi Ranganathan had the flat to herself. Her husband had taken their daughter to his parents' place in Lucknow for the long weekend after Diwali, and Aditi had stayed back in Gurugram with a board pre-read she had already rewritten four times. It was 9.40 in the evening. The board met at eleven on Monday at Pahiya's office in Sector 44, with two of the six directors joining from Singapore and San Francisco.

On the screen in front of her was a slide with a single chart: Pahiya Care's DAU/MAU, rising from 3.1 per cent in January to 9.2 per cent in October. Beside it, in a second window, was a message Sridhar Venkataraman had sent from Bengaluru at 4.12 that afternoon, which she had read six times and had not yet answered. It said, without preamble: "Before you present that chart — the March release added a background sync that writes a session event. I raised it in PAH-4471. I don't think anyone closed it. The true series may be flatter. I can't tell you how much flatter until Wednesday."

The chart was not decorative. In August 2024, Pahiya had raised ₹120 crore at a valuation of ₹2,400 crore, and the term sheet carried a second tranche of ₹60 crore contingent on the company reaching 25 lakh monthly active users and 8 per cent DAU/MAU on the Pahiya Care app by 31 December 2025. In October the reported figures had been 26.4 lakh and 9.2 per cent. Kunal Bhargava, the chief executive, had already told one of the investors, informally, that the milestone was cleared.

Aditi's problem on Monday was not really the chart. It was that she no longer believed anyone in the company, including herself, could say what Pahiya Care was for.

2. How Pahiya got here

Pahiya was founded in Gurugram in 2017 by Kunal Bhargava and two colleagues from a logistics start-up, as a marketplace matching private sellers of used cars with buyers. For three years it was asset-light: inspect, list, connect, take a fee. Revenue in FY20 was ₹61 crore.

The decision that shaped everything afterwards was taken in the second half of 2022. Competing with Cars24 and Spinny, both of which were buying cars onto their own balance sheets and selling them refurbished with a warranty, Pahiya concluded that a pure marketplace could not guarantee condition or title, and went full-stack. It began buying cars, refurbishing them at hubs in Gurugram, Pune, Hyderabad and Ahmedabad, and reselling them with a six-month warranty. Revenue rose to ₹1,180 crore in FY24 on gross terms, but the business now consumed working capital, carried inventory risk, and lived or died on transaction volume and gross margin per unit.

That constraint produced the second decision, in March 2023. Kunal's argument, made repeatedly to the board and eventually to investors, was that a used-car company had a fatal frequency problem: an Indian household changes its car roughly once in four to six years, which meant Pahiya spent heavily to acquire a customer, transacted once, and then lost the relationship entirely to service centres, insurance agents and the next platform. The answer was a "frequency ladder" — an ownership app that would keep the customer within Pahiya between transactions. Pahiya Care launched in July 2023 with challan status checks, FASTag balance and recharge, service booking through partner garages, insurance renewal, RC transfer tracking and a monthly valuation estimate for the car the customer owned.

The free utilities worked immediately in the sense that people used them. The challan check, in particular, spread by word of mouth. By late 2025 Pahiya Care had 26.4 lakh monthly actives against a cumulative transacting customer base of 3.1 lakh.

3. The industry around it

India's used-car market was, by most estimates, larger in units than the new-car market and considerably more fragmented. Organised players — Cars24, Spinny, CarDekho, OLX Autos, Maruti Suzuki True Value and Mahindra First Choice Wheels — together accounted for a minority of transactions; most cars still changed hands through neighbourhood dealers and family networks. Every organised player was solving the same trust problem: condition, title and price.

Several external structures bore directly on Pahiya Care. Ownership data came from the national vehicle registry through an authorised data aggregator, and Pahiya paid per lookup for challan and RC status. FASTag recharges ran on the NPCI rails and earned a few rupees per transaction at best. Insurance renewal was regulated by the IRDAI and Pahiya operated as a corporate agent, earning commission. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act obliged Pahiya to obtain and be able to demonstrate consent for every registry lookup it performed on a user's behalf, and the compliance team had flagged in September that consent for the "auto-refresh challan" feature — which polled the registry monthly without a fresh user action — rested on a broad consent taken at sign-up, which counsel described as "defensible but not comfortable." Used-car sales carried GST on the dealer's margin, which made gross-margin discipline unusually visible in the accounts.

Pahiya also had two non-Indian exposures. Priya Menon, in Singapore, had licensed Pahiya's inspection-and-pricing software to Sharq Auto Trading, a used-car retail group in Dubai running eleven yards, on a three-year contract worth ₹18 crore, renewable in April 2026 and carrying a ₹2.6 crore penalty if a contracted multi-yard inventory module was not delivered by then. Rohit Deshpande, in New Jersey, was running a pilot selling the same software to independent dealers in the American Northeast.

4. The situation in detail

The sequence mattered, and Aditi had written it out for herself because the meanings kept shifting.

March 2023. Farhan Siddiqui's team in Toronto built the model that justified Pahiya Care. Its central assumption was that an owner who used the app monthly would be three times more likely to transact with Pahiya at their next purchase, and that the purchase interval was 4.8 years. On those numbers the ladder paid for itself at a cost of ₹340 per active user per year.

July 2023 to December 2024. The app grew. Challan checks drove most of it. Marketing in Gurugram ran the growth loop hard through Diwali 2024 with an offer of free RC-transfer assistance for referrals.

August 2024. The Series D closed with the milestone tranche attached. Kunal had proposed the engagement milestone himself; the lead investor had accepted it in preference to a revenue milestone, which Kunal at the time regarded as a win.

March 2025. An app release added a background sync for valuation refresh. It wrote a session event. PAH-4471 was opened by an engineer, assigned to a team lead who moved to another squad in April, and never closed.

June 2025. Farhan's team ran a matched holdout on transaction propensity — Care users versus statistically matched owners who had transacted with Pahiya but never installed the app — and found no significant difference in the rate of returning to Pahiya for a second transaction within the observation period. The observation period was five months. Farhan reported the result in a weekly note. Nobody escalated it.

September 2025. Meghna Rau, the chief financial officer in Mumbai, circulated a cost breakdown showing that registry lookups, FASTag processing and the support load from free-utility users cost ₹11.4 crore annually against direct revenue from those features of ₹1.9 crore.

October 2025. The marketing team ran an in-app survey during the Diwali campaign. Sixty-two per cent of respondents said they would consider Pahiya for their next car purchase. The number went into the board pre-read.

14 November 2025. Sharq Auto Trading's chief operating officer wrote to Priya asking, politely, whether the multi-yard module would land before April, "as we are also in discussion with two other vendors."

16 November 2025, 4.12 p.m. Sridhar's message about the background sync.

5. The people

Kunal Bhargava, co-founder and chief executive, Gurugram. Position: the ladder is working and needs more investment, not less; the app is the moat. Incentive: a Series E conversation he wants to open in February, and a milestone tranche he has effectively pre-announced. Not saying: that he told the lead investor in October that the milestone was cleared, and that walking it back now would be a different kind of conversation than walking it back in January.

Aditi Ranganathan, chief product officer, Gurugram. Joined 2021 from a payments company. Position: undecided, which is itself a position when the board meets in fourteen hours. Incentive: she will own whichever metric survives Monday. Not saying: she has believed for three months that Pahiya Care serves a different person from the one who buys cars, and she has not tested it because she is not sure she wants the answer before the tranche closes.

Meghna Rau, chief financial officer, Mumbai. Position: shut the free utilities, keep insurance and service, and put the saving into inventory turns. Incentive: the unit-economics story for the Series E, and a covenant on working capital. Not saying: she has run a scenario in which the consumer app is discontinued entirely and it improves FY27 EBITDA by ₹9 crore, and she has not shared it because she expects Kunal to treat it as an attack.

Sridhar Venkataraman, vice-president of engineering, Bengaluru. Position: fix the instrumentation before anyone presents anything. Incentive: he has a platform re-architecture he has wanted funded for two quarters. Not saying: the background sync came out of his own team's sprint, and PAH-4471 sat unclosed because his team lead's move was a promotion he had pushed for.

Farhan Siddiqui, head of data science, Toronto. Position: the holdout result should be repeated with a longer window before anyone concludes anything, but the honest reading today is that Care has not yet been shown to change transaction behaviour. Incentive: methodological credibility. Not saying: the 4.8-year purchase interval in his 2023 model came from an industry report and not from Pahiya's own data, and Pahiya's own resale records now suggest the interval for its customer base is closer to 6.2 years, which would roughly halve the modelled return on the ladder.

Lena Hofmann, principal designer, Berlin. Position: the app is a bag of utilities with no spine; build a genuine ownership record — a car's health, history, documents and value in one timeline — and frequency will follow value rather than the other way round. Incentive: craft. Not saying: she has a second-round interview at another company on 24 November.

Priya Menon, head of customer success and partnerships, Singapore. Position: the software that dealers use every working day is the only part of Pahiya with honest daily engagement, and it is being starved. Incentive: her renewal number for FY27 includes Sharq. Not saying: Sharq's chief operating officer has twice raised the idea of an exclusive arrangement for the Gulf, which would be attractive to Priya and complicated for Pahiya.

Rohit Deshpande, sales head, New Jersey. Position: American independent dealers will pay per-seat for inventory and pricing tools; give him the roadmap and he will build a business. Incentive: a commission plan written against bookings. Not saying: of the six deals in his reported pipeline, two are verbal and one contact has left his company.

6. Exhibits

Exhibit 1 is the chart on Aditi's slide, and the step between March and April is the whole difficulty. Read naively, the line crosses the 8 per cent milestone in June and stays there. Read against Sridhar's message, the step coincides exactly with a release, and the dashed grey line is what nobody has yet computed.

7. Voices

"Every consumer business that matters in this country got there by becoming part of somebody's week. We sell a car once in five years. If we don't own the five years in between, we're a classifieds site with a warehouse."

Kunal Bhargava, leadership offsite, Udaipur, September 2025

"I am not against the ladder. I am against paying ₹11.4 crore a year for the privilege of being the place where people check whether they have a pending challan. Show me one rupee of incremental car margin from it and I will fund it myself."

Meghna Rau, finance review, 24 September 2025

"Point of order on the exhibit. The survey is 412 people who opened the app during a campaign that gave away a fuel voucher. I would not put it in the same deck as a 48,000-person holdout without saying which one I trust. I also would not put the holdout in without saying that five months is nothing against a six-year purchase cycle."

Farhan Siddiqui, comment on the board pre-read, 13 November 2025

"We don't have an app. We have six utilities in a drawer. A person who checks a challan is not in a relationship with us any more than someone who uses a public toilet is in a relationship with the municipality. Give me two quarters and a car-health timeline and I will show you what returning for a reason looks like."

Lena Hofmann, design review, Berlin, 6 November 2025

"Sharq's team logs into our software 11 hours a day, six days a week. Eleven yards, 340 cars in stock. That is the only product we have where people are in it every working day because their job requires it. And it is nine engineers in Pune with an unfunded module and a renewal in April."

Priya Menon, partnership review call, 11 November 2025

"Before you present that chart — the March release added a background sync that writes a session event. I raised it in PAH-4471. I don't think anyone closed it. The true series may be flatter. I can't tell you how much flatter until Wednesday."

Sridhar Venkataraman, message to Aditi, 16 November 2025, 4.12 p.m.

8. The options as Aditi sees them

Double down on the ladder. Ask the board for ₹40 crore over FY27 to build Pahiya Care into a full ownership product — Lena's car-health timeline, deeper service integration, a document vault, a loyalty construct — on the argument that the relationship between transactions is the only durable asset a used-car company can own. It protects the milestone, keeps Kunal's narrative intact, and gives Lena a reason to stay. It also commits the company further to a thesis that Exhibit 5 cannot yet support and Exhibit 4 arguably undermines.

Cut to the paying occasions. Retire the auto-refresh challan feature and the free valuation push, keep insurance, service booking and the transaction funnel, and accept that MAU falls — plausibly to five or six lakh — and that the milestone is missed. The economics improve immediately and the product becomes legible. It also means telling the board, fourteen hours from now, that a number the chief executive has already described as cleared will not be cleared, and it puts ₹60 crore into question with fourteen months of runway.

Follow the daily users. Move engineering weight to the dealer platform, fund Sharq's multi-yard module, give Rohit a roadmap for the American pilot, and let the consumer app run in maintenance. Here the users genuinely work in the product every day because their livelihood requires it, and they pay for it. It is also a different company from the one the Series D funded, sold to a different buyer, and it leaves the Indian consumer brand — the thing the valuation is built on — untended.

Aditi had written all three on a page, and then, underneath, a sentence she had not shown anyone: "All three of these assume the unit is the app. What if the unit is the car?" Pahiya knew a great deal about 68 lakh vehicles it had inspected, priced or tracked, and almost nothing about the households that owned them; a household in Pune with three vehicles counted as three registrations and one account, or sometimes three accounts. Whether that reframing led anywhere useful by eleven the next morning was another question.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The milestone is tested on 31 December 2025 against reported figures, with the investor entitled to request an independent verification of the metric definition. Cash on hand is ₹146 crore, fourteen months at current burn, and the Series E conversation Kunal wants to open in February will be read against whatever is said on Monday. Headcount is frozen until March. The Sharq contract renews in April 2026 with a ₹2.6 crore penalty attached to the undelivered module and ₹6 crore of revenue at risk. The auto-refresh challan feature rests on a sign-up consent that counsel has called defensible but not comfortable under the DPDP Act, and the compliance team has asked for a decision by January either way. Sridhar cannot restate the analytics series before Wednesday. Lena's interview is on the twenty-fourth. And the board pre-read, containing Exhibit 1 and the 62 per cent survey result, was circulated on Thursday and has already been read.

10. Questions for discussion

1. Using Exhibits 1 to 4, what would you say Pahiya Care's stickiness actually is, and what would you need in order to say it with confidence?

2. What is the natural frequency of each job in Exhibit 3, and which of those jobs is Pahiya genuinely serving as against generating?

3. Exhibit 5 contains two studies that point in opposite directions. How should Aditi weigh them, and what study would she have to commission to settle the question — and how long would it take?

4. Kunal's frequency-ladder thesis is a claim that cheap frequent interactions convert into rare expensive ones. What evidence in the case supports it, what undermines it, and what would falsify it?

5. The Series D milestone was chosen by the company itself. What does the choice of an engagement milestone over a revenue milestone do to a product organisation over fifteen months, and what should Aditi do about a metric that has become a covenant?

6. What should Aditi say at eleven o'clock on Monday morning — about the chart, about the background sync, about the milestone, and about what Pahiya is for — and what would she be committing the company to by saying it?

Sunday, 11.20 p.m.

Aditi made tea and did not drink it. She had three versions of the slide now. The first was the one in the pre-read, which the directors had already seen and which, if Sridhar was right, overstated a number on which ₹60 crore turned. The second removed the chart entirely and replaced it with Exhibit 4, which was honest and which would be read as an ambush of her own chief executive in front of the board. The third kept the chart and added a footnote about the March release in nine-point type, which was the coward's version and which she would be asked about in the first two minutes by the director in Singapore, who read footnotes.

At 11.20 she typed a reply to Sridhar — "How flat is flat? Best guess, no caveats, tonight." — and then deleted it, because a best guess with no caveats was how the company had got here in the first place. She looked at the sentence she had written under the three options and read it again. The unit is the car. Or the household. Or the transaction. Or the five years in between, which nobody had ever measured because nobody had agreed what to count.

Her phone showed 11.41. The board met in eleven hours and nineteen minutes, and she had not yet decided which version to send.

Stickiness and Natural Frequency

How sticky is the product, relative to how often the problem naturally occurs?

A number that will not hold still

On the second Monday of March 2024, Ananya Rao opened the analytics dashboard at RituCare, a Bengaluru-based women's health app with 2.1 million registered users, and found the number she had been dreading. DAU/MAU — daily active users divided by monthly active users, the ratio product teams call "stickiness" — sat at 11%. The board deck for Thursday's meeting already had a slide comparing RituCare to Instagram, above 50%, and to Swiggy, near 20%. The chairperson's margin note read: "Why are we a third as sticky as a food app? Fix this before the Series C conversation."

Ananya had eighteen months of data and a growing unease about the question itself. RituCare's core function was cycle tracking: a woman logs her period, her symptoms, perhaps a basal temperature reading, and the app predicts her next cycle and fertile window. A typical user's cycle is 28 days long. She has perhaps four to six days each month where logging is genuinely useful — the days she is bleeding, and the day or two around ovulation if she is trying to conceive. For roughly twenty-two days of every cycle, opening RituCare and finding nothing new to log is not disengagement. It is the product working as intended. If Ananya spent the next quarter's roadmap chasing Instagram's DAU/MAU, she would be optimizing RituCare into something that pings its users daily whether or not their bodies have anything to report — trading trust for a vanity metric two weeks before a fundraising round that depended on investors reading the metrics correctly. Getting this wrong in either direction — dismissing the board's concern, or chasing a number that measures the wrong thing — would cost her credibility with one audience or product integrity with the other. She had eleven days to build the argument.

The idea, precisely

Stickiness, measured as DAU/MAU, is the fraction of a product's monthly active users who are also active on a typical day within that month. If 300,000 of RituCare's 2.7 million monthly active users open the app on an average day, DAU/MAU is 300,000 divided by 2.7 million, or 11.1%. The metric was popularized inside Facebook in the mid-2000s, where engineers needed a single number to track whether a growing user base was also a returning one — a company can grow its monthly total while its daily engagement quietly rots, and DAU/MAU was built to catch that divergence early. Read alone, a rising DAU/MAU has come to signal "more engaged," and product teams have absorbed the shorthand that higher is unambiguously better.

The correction this topic teaches is that DAU/MAU is not a measure of engagement quality in isolation — it is a measure of how closely a product's observed usage rhythm matches its user base's natural rhythm for the problem the product solves. The single sentence Ananya could say in the boardroom without sounding glib: "Our stickiness ceiling is set by how often the problem the product solves actually recurs, not by how good the product is — so the right benchmark is a product with our frequency, not the highest DAU/MAU in the industry." A cycle-tracking app, a life-insurance-comparison tool, and a home-loan EMI calculator all have low natural frequency built into the problem itself; comparing their DAU/MAU to a messaging app is comparing answers to different questions.

How it actually works

The mechanics start with getting DAU and MAU defined identically before any ratio is computed — a step Ananya found practitioners at RituCare had quietly skipped. DAU is the count of unique users performing a defined "active" action on a given day; MAU is the count performing that same action at least once in a trailing 30-day window. If "active" means "opened the app" for one metric and "logged a symptom" for the other, the ratio compares two different behaviors and is meaningless before it is even graphed. RituCare's engineering team, it turned out, counted a push-notification tap as a DAU event but not an MAU event, quietly inflating the numerator relative to the denominator for months.

Once the definitions match, the next step — the one practitioners most often leave implicit — is estimating natural frequency before judging the ratio. This means asking, independent of the product entirely: how often does the underlying problem or need actually arise for a typical user? For a menstrual cycle, the honest answer is "once every 28 days for the core event, with a handful of higher-frequency days around it." For a grocery-delivery app, it might be twice a week. For a home-loan servicing app, once a month, when the EMI is due. This natural frequency sets a ceiling — call it the theoretical maximum stickiness — against which the observed DAU/MAU should be judged, rather than against an industry-wide average pulled from products with an entirely different natural rhythm.

The final step is choosing the right observation window to match that frequency. A product used on a natural monthly cycle will always look unstick on a DAU/MAU7 basis (daily actives over 7-day actives) because most of its real users have nothing to do on most days. The fix is not to change the product's behavior to manufacture daily activity; it is to change the interval of analysis — DAU/MAU, WAU/MAU (weekly actives over monthly), or even a bespoke "cycle-period actives over monthly actives" — so that the ratio's numerator window is close to the natural frequency of the underlying need, and the resulting number can be compared honestly across products with similar rhythms.

A worked example

Ananya pulled RituCare's raw counts for February 2024, a 29-day month. Monthly active users, defined as anyone who opened the app or received a push notification they acted on, totalled 2,700,000. She computed average daily actives by summing unique daily actives across the 29 days and dividing by 29, getting 299,700, which she rounded to 300,000. DAU/MAU: 300,000 / 2,700,000 = 0.1111, or 11.1%.

To make the ratio meaningful, she needed the natural-frequency ceiling. RituCare's own cohort data showed the median user logs on 5.4 distinct days per 28-day cycle: the days of bleeding (typically 5) plus roughly one day around predicted ovulation. If every one of RituCare's users behaved exactly like the median and logged on exactly 5.4 of 28 days, uniformly spread, the theoretical DAU/MAU ceiling would be 5.4/28 = 19.3%. Measured against an industry-wide benchmark of "good" DAU/MAU (20%+, drawn from social and messaging products), 11.1% looks like underperformance. Measured against RituCare's own natural-frequency ceiling of 19.3%, 11.1% means the product is capturing 11.1/19.3 = 57.5% of its theoretical maximum — a meaningfully different and far more actionable number.

MetricValue
Monthly active users (Feb 2024)2,700,000
Average daily active users300,000
Observed DAU/MAU11.1%
Median logging days per 28-day cycle5.4
Natural-frequency ceiling (5.4/28)19.3%
Share of theoretical ceiling captured57.5%

Now the second pass, changing one input: suppose RituCare ships a feature that lets users log daily basal body temperature for those actively trying to conceive, and 18% of the user base adopts it, logging on all 28 days instead of 5.4. The blended median logging days per user becomes (0.82 × 5.4) + (0.18 × 28) = 4.43 + 5.04 = 9.47 days per 28-day cycle. The new natural-frequency ceiling is 9.47/28 = 33.8%, and if adoption behavior holds at the same 57.5% capture rate, the new expected DAU/MAU is roughly 19.4% — nearly double the original figure, achieved without a single "engagement hack," because the underlying natural frequency of the problem itself changed for a subset of users. This is the crucial move: the lever that moved DAU/MAU was a change in what problem the product solves for whom, not a change in notification cadence.

The nuances a learner must sit with

Stickiness is not loyalty

A user who opens RituCare daily but has stopped trusting its predictions is not more loyal than one who opens it five days a month and renews her subscription every year. DAU/MAU captures frequency of contact, not depth of trust or willingness to pay. Two products can have identical stickiness and completely different retention curves twelve months out.

The denominator hides its own assumptions

MAU counting rules — whether a notification tap counts, whether a background sync counts, whether the window is a calendar month or a trailing 30 days — change the ratio by several points without any real change in user behavior. Any cross-company or cross-quarter comparison of DAU/MAU is worthless unless both sides used the same operational definition of "active."

Natural frequency is a distribution, not a single number

Treating "once every 28 days" as true of every RituCare user erases the real variance: some users have 21-day cycles, some have irregular ones precisely because of a condition the app should help them manage. A single ceiling number is a useful simplification for a boardroom slide, not a substitute for looking at the underlying histogram when making product decisions.

What it is routinely confused with

Teams frequently conflate DAU/MAU with retention. Retention asks whether a specific user from a specific cohort is still present N days after signup; DAU/MAU is a snapshot ratio across the whole active base at one point in time. A product can hold flat, healthy 90-day retention while its DAU/MAU declines because its user base has simply grown to include more low-frequency segments — nothing about individual users got worse.

The conditions under which the comparison works

Comparing DAU/MAU across products only works when natural frequency is comparable. RituCare against a period-tracking competitor is fair. RituCare against a step-counting fitness app, even though both are "health apps," is not, because the natural frequency of the underlying behaviors — menstrual cycles versus daily movement — differs by an order of magnitude.

What it cannot tell you, however well you apply it

DAU/MAU, even normalized for natural frequency, says nothing about whether the product is solving the problem well on the days a user does show up. A woman who opens RituCare on exactly the right five days but receives an inaccurate ovulation prediction has a "healthy" stickiness number and a failing product. Stickiness measures rhythm, not quality of the interaction within that rhythm.

The interval choice itself can be gamed

A team under pressure to raise DAU/MAU can simply redefine "active" more loosely — counting an impression instead of a tap — and watch the ratio rise with zero change in real behavior. A thoughtful newcomer should always ask what event defines "active" before trusting any DAU/MAU figure.

Multi-need products break the single-frequency model

A product bundling several jobs with different natural frequencies — RituCare's cycle tracking plus its telehealth booking plus its symptom forum — has no single natural frequency at all. A blended DAU/MAU across all three obscures which job drives daily engagement and which drags the average down.

Consumer, B2B, marketplace, and scale

In consumer products, natural frequency is usually set by biology, habit, or a recurring life event, and it is relatively stable — people do not suddenly need groceries twice as often. In B2B products the natural frequency is set by a business process and is often lumpier: Samay Enterprises, a payroll-and-compliance SaaS used by mid-sized Indian manufacturers, sees finance teams engage intensely for three days around each month's payroll run and barely at all otherwise, producing a DAU/MAU that looks alarming until overlaid on the payroll calendar. Marketplaces add a second complication: buyers and sellers can have entirely different natural frequencies on one platform. At Kaalchakra Freight, a trucking-capacity marketplace, drivers check the app several times a day for loads while shippers post a consignment perhaps twice a week — a single blended DAU/MAU would misrepresent both sides, so the platform tracks the ratio separately for each.

Company stage matters too. An early-stage product often shows an artificially high DAU/MAU because its first cohort is disproportionately enthusiastic early adopters; as Prahar Analytics, a B2B data-visualization tool, scaled from 200 pilot customers to 8,000 paying accounts, its DAU/MAU fell from 34% to 14%, not because the product got worse but because later cohorts were ordinary finance analysts opening dashboards weekly, exactly the frequency their job required.

Common mistakes

The first mistake is benchmarking against a famous product instead of a frequency-matched one. Symptom: a team comparing its DAU/MAU to Instagram or WhatsApp regardless of what the product does. Misunderstanding: treating stickiness as an absolute virtue rather than a relative-to-frequency one. Cheapest diagnostic: ask the team to name the problem's natural frequency before naming a benchmark competitor.

The second is chasing DAU/MAU with notification volume. Symptom: a rising DAU/MAU alongside flat renewals and rising opt-outs. Misunderstanding: treating the metric as the goal rather than a proxy for genuine need. Cheapest diagnostic: check whether the rise in daily actives correlates with the specific action the product exists to support, not a bare app open.

The third is inconsistent "active" definitions across dashboards. Symptom: two teams reporting different DAU/MAU numbers for the same month. Misunderstanding: assuming everyone means the same event by "active." Cheapest diagnostic: a five-minute check that both numerator and denominator use an identical event definition and window.

The fourth is ignoring segment-level frequency inside one product. Symptom: a flat, mediocre blended DAU/MAU that never responds to product changes. Misunderstanding: analyzing one company-wide number when the product serves several jobs with different rhythms. Cheapest diagnostic: split DAU/MAU by feature or declared intent and check whether segments tell a different story than the average.

What good looks like

At Samay Enterprises, the payroll SaaS, a new head of analytics faced the same board pressure Ananya did eighteen months earlier. Instead of arguing against the concern, she built a one-page memo showing the payroll calendar overlaid on daily active usage, demonstrating that 71% of monthly logins clustered in the four days around the 25th to the 1st of each month — exactly the payroll cycle. She then proposed tracking "active-days-during-payroll-window over total-payroll-window-days" as the primary stickiness metric, alongside a secondary, honestly low, all-month DAU/MAU for context. The board accepted a revised target within one meeting because the argument was structural, evidence-based, and did not ask them to simply trust a lower number.

The decision, and what to carry forward

Ananya built the same kind of memo: the natural-frequency ceiling calculation, the 57.5%-of-ceiling framing, and the second-pass arithmetic showing that the basal-temperature feature could roughly double DAU/MAU by genuinely serving a higher-frequency need for a real subset of users, rather than by manufacturing false urgency for everyone. She recommended the board track two numbers going forward: DAU/MAU against RituCare's own natural-frequency ceiling, reported quarterly as "share of theoretical maximum captured," and a second, cycle-relative metric — active days per user per cycle — that would not collapse when a user's cycle length itself varied. The board approved both, and the Series C conversation proceeded on RituCare's own terms rather than Instagram's.

What Ananya should study next is the topic this one unlocks: engagement loops and habit formation, which asks how a product designer can, ethically, raise a real natural frequency — as the basal-temperature feature did — rather than merely simulate one. Two questions worth sitting with: for a product you know well, what is the honest natural frequency of the problem it solves, and would you be embarrassed to say that number out loud in a board meeting? And when a stickiness number moves, can you say with evidence whether the underlying need changed, or only the measurement of it did?

Metrics, Analytics & Experimentation · Product Analytics & Data Practice

Stickiness and Natural Frequency

How sticky is the product, relative to how often the problem naturally occurs — and what happens when the ratio used to answer that question cannot arithmetically do so?

1. Two rooms, one ratio

On 14 August 2026, Meghna Iyer, VP of Product and Analytics at Jwaar Wealth, a Bengaluru investing app with 6.4 million monthly active users, sat in a pre-read for the September board meeting at the slide she had argued about for three weeks: DAU/MAU 12.2%, flat for five quarters. The growth team's attached proposal was a daily markets briefing — a 9:10 a.m. push with an index move — projected to lift the ratio to 19%. Jwaar Wealth would file a draft prospectus in February 2027, after which "monthly active user" became a disclosed, audited, frozen quantity.

Meghna could decompose the 12.2% and disliked what it implied. Jwaar Wealth served two populations sharing a login and nothing else. Roughly 4.9 million were systematic-investment-plan holders, whose real need to open the app arose when the ₹5,000 debit landed and again when a statement appeared. Their stickiness was 5.8%. The other 1.5 million were self-directed traders transacting on market days, at 33%. Add 284,000 to 495,000: 779,000 daily actives against 6.4 million monthly. The blend described no user, and had been flat for five quarters while both segments improved, because the SIP base grew faster.

Three weeks later, on 3 September 2026, Srinivas Prabhu, Chief Product Officer of Bhaata Systems in Hyderabad, was in the fourth day of diligence with a private-equity buyer. Bhaata sold quality-management software to Indian pharmaceutical manufacturers — batch records, deviation and CAPA workflows, the trail a USFDA or CDSCO inspector asks for: 190 accounts, 41,000 seats, ₹212 crore of ARR, 118% net revenue retention. The buyer's memo carried one adverse line: "Engagement materially below SaaS benchmark: DAU/MAU 9.0% vs. 25% median for vertical SaaS at scale. Risk of shelfware." The proposed consequence was half a turn off the multiple: ₹98 crore.

Srinivas's difficulty was the mirror image of Meghna's. Usage was low not because the product was weak but because Bhaata had spent three years removing the need to log in: a 2024 auto-routing release cut the sessions needed to close a deviation from 6.2 to 2.4 while median closure time fell from 19 days to 6. Every unit of that improvement pushed DAU/MAU down. His product council's answer was a "morning quality huddle" dashboard every plant manager would be expected to open — a ritual inserted into a shift that had not asked for one.

Two competent practitioners, two credible boards, one ratio — and in both rooms it was being asked a question it cannot answer without a companion model of how often the underlying problem occurs.

2. The idea, and the quarrel inside it

Stickiness is average daily active users over monthly active users for the same period, under an identical definition of "active." Natural frequency is the rate at which the problem the product solves recurs in the user's life or work, measured independently of the product: payroll runs for a payroll system, batch releases for Bhaata, SIP debits for Jwaar Wealth's investors. Observed stickiness is jointly determined by natural frequency and by the product's capture of it; reading the ratio without the first term is like reading headcount without an industry.

The metric's product-analytics lineage is short. DAU and MAU became standard disclosure through the consumer-internet IPOs of 2011 and 2012: Zynga's S-1 made the pair and their ratio a reported quantity, and its decline there was the early tell of decay; Facebook's February 2012 S-1 reported 845 million monthly and 483 million daily actives for December 2011, a ratio of 57% that became the ceiling against which every consumer product was measured. Fred Wilson's 2011 "30/10/10" heuristic hardened the folklore into a rule of thumb, and Facebook's internal "L28" notation — how many of the last 28 days a user was active — later spread through the analytics vendors.

The natural frequency half is older and comes from marketing science. Andrew Ehrenberg's work from 1959 onward established that purchase frequency in a category follows a negative binomial distribution remarkably stable across brands and time: how often people buy toothpaste is a property of toothpaste, not of Colgate. Schmittlein, Morrison and Colombo's 1987 "Counting Your Customers" supplied the apparatus for what matters most here: telling a customer who has stopped from one who is merely irregular. That literature had already shown observed frequency to be a mixture of a rate and a dropout process, which a single ratio cannot separate.

Four schools now hold recognisably different positions, and the disagreement is real rather than terminological.

The frequency-is-destiny school holds that natural frequency is a property of the problem, set by the world; a team can capture more of it but cannot change it. They will sign: "benchmark only within a frequency class; a tax product and a messaging product are not comparable." They will not sign: "a good roadmap can double a product's natural frequency," which they read as a category error dressed as ambition.

The frequency-is-designed school, descended from habit design and the social-gaming era, holds that natural frequency is a property of the job set, and the job set is a product decision. They will sign: "expanding into an adjacent higher-frequency job is a legitimate and often the only way to raise engagement." They will not sign: "notification cadence is the same kind of lever as job expansion."

The distribution-first school regards the ratio itself as the problem: any quotient of a one-day over a thirty-day window compresses a distribution into a scalar, non-linearly. They will sign: "report the L30 histogram and the return-interval distribution." They will not sign: "stickiness normalised for natural frequency is a sufficient summary," because the normalisation inherits the compression.

The outcome-frequency school, dominant in enterprise software, holds that sessions are not the unit of value — jobs completed per account per period are — and that session-based stickiness punishes automation. They will sign Srinivas's position exactly. They will not sign: "low login frequency is never a warning sign," because in seat-priced software, seats that never log in get cut at renewal.

3. Mechanics: the arithmetic that practitioners skip

Begin with the step almost nobody documents: fixing the event. DAU and MAU must count the same action over windows of different length. Meghna found three live definitions — an app open, a screen with portfolio value rendered, and any authenticated API call, which swept in the background price refresh the OS triggers on an installed app. The third produced a DAU 34% higher than the first. The definition must be a sentence a stranger could reimplement.

The second step separates practice from folklore: build the natural-frequency model from a source outside the product. Bhaata could do this exactly, because pharmaceutical manufacturing generates the events. Across 190 accounts the team counted 18,400 batch releases and 3,100 deviation closures a month, each with mandated touchpoints: maker and checker on a release, three roles on a deviation. Summed over the seat base, the process implied an average monthly active user had cause to be in the system on 3.1 days: a ceiling of 3.1/30 = 10.3%. Against 9.0% observed, Bhaata was capturing 87% of what its customers' calendars permitted. The 25% benchmark was not demanding; it was unreachable.

The third step surprises most: DAU/MAU is not an average of individual stickiness. Let user i have probability pi of being active on a given day. Average DAU is the sum of pi. MAU is the count active at least once in thirty days — for independent daily draws, the sum of 1 − (1 − pi)30. The denominator saturates: above roughly p = 0.15 a user is in MAU with near-certainty and further activity raises only the numerator, while below it the denominator discounts her. Two products with identical mean usage can differ twofold on distribution shape alone.

The demonstration uses two types with identical long-run usage. A regular user is active exactly one day in thirty; a bursty user, three consecutive days once in ninety. The regular user appears in every window, contributing 1/30 to DAU and 1 to MAU: 3.3%. The bursty user appears in about one window in three, contributing the same 1/30 to DAU but only 1/3 to MAU: 10%. Same annual behaviour, three times the stickiness.

The fourth step is choosing the window from the data rather than from convention, which is what interval analysis does: take every pair of consecutive active days, compute the gap, plot the survival curve. For Jwaar Wealth's traders the median return gap was 2 days and the 80th percentile 6; for SIP holders, 27 and 32. The working rule is to set the numerator window near the 80th percentile, so a user behaving normally is counted present. That gives traders a weekly window and SIP holders a monthly one — the two cannot share a stickiness metric.

A fifth mechanic is growth deflation. A trailing thirty-day MAU includes users acquired part-way through the window, who had less than a month in which to be active. Suppose a settled user is active six days a month — 20% individually — and users acquired within the window average half that contribution. If 30% of MAU is new, the blend is 0.7 × 20% + 0.3 × 10% = 17%, against 20% for an identical product that has stopped growing. Acquisition mechanically depresses the metric; a slowdown flatters it.

4. When the idea applies, stated as claims you can test

The framework rests on four conditions, each of which can be checked rather than assumed.

Claim one: the recurrence of the job is observable independently of the product. Bhaata passes — batch releases and deviations exist in the customer's ERP whether or not Bhaata is installed. Jwaar Wealth passes for the SIP cohort, whose debits are external facts, and fails for traders, where the need to trade is partly created by the product's own market feed. Where the job is product-generated, the ceiling calculation is circular.

Claim two: the population is homogeneous enough for a single ceiling to mean something. Bhaata fails: 3.1 days conceals line QA officers in the system most working days alongside audit reviewers who appear twice a quarter. Jwaar Wealth fails more obviously. Both must compute ceilings per segment or admit the ceiling is a weighted fiction.

Claim three: usage is the mechanism of value, not the cost of receiving it. For a media product the session is the value; for a compliance workflow it is friction tolerated to obtain an outcome. Where usage is a cost, higher stickiness is worse, normalised or not, and the right metric is outcomes per account per period against the customer's own process volume.

Claim four: the definition of "active" is stable across the comparison being made. Neither protagonist passed initially — Meghna had three definitions inside one company, and the diligence team could not produce the definition behind its own benchmark. A comparison with unstated definitions is not weak; it is not a comparison.

The apparatus turns harmful when a team uses low frequency as a permanent explanation. Low frequency explains a low ratio; it does not explain a falling one, a segment that never returns, or a capture rate of 40%. "We are a low-frequency product" must arrive with a capture number attached.

5. Hard edges

Multi-product portfolios break the metric at the login. Account-level DAU/MAU rises with the number of products a customer buys regardless of whether any is used well: a payments tab would lift Jwaar Wealth's account-level figure from 12.2% to an estimated 24% while doing nothing for the investing product. Mature companies compute stickiness per product line on a product-specific event — though the figure they quote on earnings calls is usually the account-level one, because it is larger.

Two-sided platforms have two natural frequencies and no legitimate blend. Kinaara Fleet Systems, a Coimbatore load-matching and telematics platform, measured 46% stickiness among drivers, 11% among fleet owners reviewing utilisation weekly, and 7% among shipper procurement staff. The blended 19% moved more with supply-side growth than with any product change. Kinaara replaced it with per-side coverage metrics — share of driver-shifts with a load view, share of consignments whose shipper opened tracking — frequency-normalised by construction, their denominators counting job instances rather than people.

Regulated environments produce compliance-driven actives that look like engagement. Several of Bhaata's customers mandate a daily electronic sign-off, so those users appear in DAU every working day whether or not the software helped. Srinivas's team tagged mandated events and reported both ways; the gap — 9.0% including them, 6.4% excluding — was the more useful number, because renewal risk lives in the voluntary portion.

Hardware-plus-software inverts the sign outright. Velamitra Care, a Chennai company selling a connected blood-pressure and single-lead ECG cuff to cardiac patients, saw app stickiness fall from 21% to 13% after shipping automatic background sync, while readings captured per patient-week rose from 3.1 to 5.8. The opens that vanished were patients checking whether yesterday's reading had uploaded — anxiety traffic created by an earlier defect. For companion apps a stickiness fall is ambiguous between "the hardware works now" and "the patient stopped caring"; only the device's own event stream separates them.

AI-native products are where the field is most confused, for two reasons pulling opposite ways. Assistants have high natural frequency because their job set is unbounded, and early stickiness is further inflated by exploration traffic that decays. Agentic products have the opposite property: the better the agent, the less the human appears, and a product whose agent runs unattended overnight can deliver more value per account while its DAU collapses. Both produce the same dashboard shape.

At the organisational seam the fight is over the denominator. Finance wants MAU stable because contracts are priced against it; growth wants it permissive because it is their headline. Those preferences produced Meghna's three definitions. What mature companies actually do, as distinct from what their documentation claims, is freeze one definition when it becomes externally disclosed and quietly keep a stricter internal series for product decisions.

6. Nine distinctions that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

The denominator censors hardest exactly where you are measuring. The tell is respectable stickiness alongside poor cohort retention: the window excludes users who have drifted, so the ratio is computed over survivors. An expert recomputes it over a fixed signup cohort. MAU is not everyone who uses the product; it is everyone caught by a thirty-day net whose mesh is set by the distribution you are trying to characterise.

Stickiness rises when you lose your least frequent users. Churning the low-frequency tail removes more from the denominator than the numerator. The tell is stickiness up with absolute DAU flat and MAU down. An expert never reads the ratio without both absolute series beside it, and treats any improvement accompanied by a falling denominator as a contraction until proven otherwise.

Mix dominates behaviour at scale and can invert it. Jwaar Wealth's five flat quarters concealed SIP stickiness rising from 5.2% to 5.8% and trader stickiness from 31% to 33%, while the blend held at 12.2% because SIP users went from 68% to 77% of the base — Simpson's paradox in product costume. The diagnostic is to recompute the blend at prior-period weights, which yields 13.6% and locates 1.4 points of flatness in mix rather than product.

Growth rate is baked into the ratio. A product adding 30% of its MAU each month reports roughly three points less stickiness than its own steady state. The tell is stickiness that improves in the quarter after a marketing pullback. Experts report the ratio only for users past their activation window.

The unit of natural frequency is the job instance, not the user. The tell is a stable stickiness figure with feature-level usage churning underneath. Experts model frequency per job and derive user expectations from each account's job mix. Bhaata's ceiling therefore differs by customer: a site running 400 batches a month has a structurally stickier seat base than one running 60, and ranking the two on engagement without that adjustment produces a false renewal-risk order.

Better products sometimes need fewer visits, and the metric cannot tell you which case you are in. What distinguishes healthy decline from disengagement is whether outcome volume held: Velamitra's readings rose while opens fell; Bhaata's closures accelerated while sessions fell. The obvious reading — that any fall in engagement is bad — is wrong for every product whose job is to remove work.

Return-interval distributions are usually bimodal, so the mean is a fiction. The tell is an L30 histogram with mass at both ends and a hollow middle. On such a base, average active days per month corresponds to no real user, and a ceiling computed from it is meaningless.

Notification-induced activity is a loan against the denominator. The tell is a rising ratio with rising opt-outs. The obvious reading — that the campaign worked, because the ratio rose at once — is wrong: the numerator responds in days and the denominator in months, so the metric flatters the intervention for as long as it takes to become irreversible.

A capture rate above 100% means the model is wrong, not that the product is extraordinary. Jwaar Wealth's SIP segment shows 5.8% against a naive ceiling of 5.0%. The excess is unmodelled jobs — crash-anxiety checks, tax-season document pulls, a spouse's portfolio — plus the censoring of Figure 2. Treat a capture rate near unity as a signal to enumerate the jobs again.

7. How this differs by product type and company stage

In consumer products natural frequency is set by biology, habit or an external calendar and is hard to move; the honest levers are capture within the existing rhythm and expansion of the job set. In B2B, frequency is set by a business process the customer can itself change, which gives the vendor an unusual lever — Bhaata can raise a customer's natural frequency by moving more of its quality process onto the platform, lifting stickiness as a side effect of revenue rather than a substitute for it. Platforms have per-side frequencies that must never be blended. For hardware, the software layer's stickiness is interpretable only against device telemetry. For AI products, nobody yet knows what a healthy trajectory looks like, because exploration decay and automation-driven session reduction are confounded in every available dataset.

Stage changes the reading. Early on, stickiness is a composition artefact: the first users are enthusiasts, and the 30–40% ratios seed-stage products report decay towards the category norm, so the signal is not the level but its stability within a fixed cohort. At growth stage the metric is dominated by mix and deflation and should be segmented and cohort-fixed or not reported. At scale, and around a listing, the definition becomes a governance object, and a permissive early choice is paid for forever.

Kinaara Fleet Systems, Oct 2025 – Jun 2026. Driver-side stickiness fell five points while loads accepted per driver-week rose by half. Decomposition attributed the fall entirely to expansion into Vidarbha and north Karnataka, where new drivers sat in a 60-day onboarding ramp; drivers acquired before October 2025 were at 49%, up three points. When a ratio moves during expansion, compute the fixed-cohort version first.

Velamitra Care, Jan – Sep 2025. The eight-point fall triggered a proposal for a daily reminder. The analytics lead pulled device telemetry instead and found readings captured had nearly doubled. What settled it was a survey of the users whose opens had fallen most: 71% said they had previously opened the app "to check the reading had gone through." Before treating a session decline as disengagement, classify the sessions that disappeared.

Lehariya Live, Indore, Feb 2024 – Nov 2025 — the failure. A vernacular short-video and creator-commerce app with 11 million MAU set a company objective to raise DAU/MAU from 18% to 25% in two quarters. The mechanism chosen was notification volume: from 2.1 to 6.8 pushes per user per day. The ratio hit 27% in eleven weeks. Then, in sequence: opt-outs rose from 9% to 34%, uninstalls rose 40%, and from month five MAU — which the campaign had grown 9%, since re-engagement revived dormant users — fell 14% over two quarters, taking the ratio with it. The numerator responds in days, the denominator in months, so the ratio reported success for a quarter before reporting failure. The cost was a Series C completed fourteen months late at roughly ₹300 crore below the prior term sheet. Recovery meant cutting notification volume 71%, accepting 19% stickiness, and adopting two guard metrics: a notification-free DAU series, and a rule that no engagement objective ships without a paired ninety-day MAU floor.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

The first live disagreement is whether natural frequency is a constraint or a choice. The destiny school points to Ehrenberg's empirical regularity and to the fact that no cycle-tracking app has ever reached messaging-app frequency. The design school points to products that demonstrably changed their own frequency by adding a job: payments inside a messaging app, video inside a commerce app. For destiny to be wrong, one would have to show a product that raised frequency substantially without entering a new category; for design to be wrong, that such expansions are always separate products sharing a login.

The second is whether low-frequency products should report DAU/MAU at all. For: boards will compute it anyway from disclosed figures, and a team that refuses loses control of the framing. Against: publishing a number you have just spent a memo explaining trains the organisation to manage it. The strongest anti-reporting position is that Bhaata should disclose batch releases per account and closure time and decline the ratio; the strongest pro position is that this reads as evasion to a buyer, and evasion is priced.

The third, with least evidence on either side, concerns AI products. One camp holds that falling session frequency in an agentic product is unambiguously good — the work is being done without the human — and that outcome metrics will displace session metrics within a few years. The other holds that reduced contact is how trust and switching costs erode, and that presence has option value independent of work done. Settling it needs churn data on agentic products at three-year tenure, which does not yet exist.

11. What mastery looks like

A student of this topic can define DAU/MAU, cite the frequency argument and produce a ceiling calculation. Someone who has internalised it behaves differently in four ways. They never quote the ratio without the two absolute series and the segment weights beside it, because they have been burned by mix. They ask what external event stream sets the frequency of the problem, and will say "we cannot compute a ceiling here" rather than manufacture one. They treat a favourable movement with the same suspicion as an unfavourable one. And they distinguish changing the metric from changing the business: they will argue for adding a genuinely higher-frequency job, refuse to argue for a notification schedule, and explain why two proposals that move the same number by the same amount are not the same proposal.

12. The decisions

Meghna declined the daily markets briefing and proposed that Jwaar Wealth stop reporting a blended stickiness figure internally before the definition was frozen for the prospectus. Three parts: one written definition of "active" — an authenticated session with a user-initiated screen view, excluding background refresh — adopted at once, so the disclosed series would have twelve consistent months by February; segment-level stickiness against segment-level ceilings as the internal engagement metric; and, as the single growth initiative, a tax-and-statements workstream targeting a real, externally dated job. She accepted that the headline ratio would stay near 12% into the listing.

Srinivas did report the ratio, with three numbers around it: the 10.3% ceiling and its derivation from customer batch and deviation volumes, the 87% capture rate, and the split between mandated and voluntary sessions. He also surfaced the figure he had been most reluctant to give — stickiness for the plant-QA population alone, ceiling near 67%, capture 61% — which located the genuine product risk in a population the blend had hidden. The buyer's revised memo replaced the shelfware language with a note on concentration in high-batch-volume accounts: a real risk, and a different one.

Discussion questions. First: Meghna's decision leaves Jwaar Wealth listing with a stickiness figure a third of the consumer-internet norm, at a moment when the underwriters would prefer otherwise. Under what circumstances would you overrule her, and what would you need to believe about the tax-and-statements workstream to do so? Second: Srinivas volunteered a segment-level number that exposed a weakness the buyer had not found — sound negotiation or avoidable concession, and does your answer change if the buyer is strategic rather than financial? Third: design the smallest set of guard metrics that would have stopped Lehariya Live's campaign in week six rather than month five.

13. Going deeper

  • Retention curves and the PMF signal — the curve tells you whether the low-frequency base is stable or draining, which the ratio cannot.
  • Engagement loops and habit — how natural frequency is legitimately raised, and what separates job expansion from attention extraction.
  • Constructing a funnel — where job instances, the denominator of every ceiling, are defined and counted.
  • Reading drop-off — a capture rate below ceiling is a drop-off problem in disguise; this finds the step losing the return visit.
  • Defining activation (the aha moment) — a slow activation ramp depresses stickiness for as long as acquisition grows.
  • Cohort analysis — the only clean way to remove mix and growth artefacts from any engagement ratio.
  • Feature adoption analysis — the technique for measuring per-job frequencies separately.
  • Segmenting users in analytics — a blended stickiness figure averages incommensurable populations; segmentation is the remedy.
